cherry.name: BITSTAMP
cherry.place: Founded in Slovenia, registered in Luxembourg
cherry.takenLong: Just under 19,000 BTC (18,866) from one operational wallet
cherry.how: One of the exchange's operational (hot) wallets was compromised on 4 January 2015.
cherry.lesson: Keep only a small share of customer coins online and the rest offline.
cherry.outcome: Trading paused, then reopened nearly a week later; offline reserves covered customers.
cherry.note: Now considered the world's longest-running crypto exchange (Wikipedia, uncited there). The exact 18,866 BTC figure is from the Coinspeaker headline; Wikipedia says "less than 19,000" and gives the ~$5M only in cited headlines.

sources.title: Help Net Security: Bitstamp suspends service in wake of compromise
Coinspeaker: Bitstamp claims 18,866 BTC lost in hot wallet hack

lemon.name: CRYPTOPIA
lemon.takenLong: About NZ$24 million (roughly 10% of its assets), mostly Ethereum and ERC-20 tokens, from hot wallets; up to 900,000 users affected
lemon.usdText: about NZ$24 million at the time
lemon.how: Suspicious hot-wallet activity pointed to a compromised private key; the theft ran on for weeks.
lemon.lesson: A hot wallet is a target: keep its balance small and watched.
lemon.outcome: The firm went into liquidation in May 2019; liquidators began returning funds in December 2024.
lemon.note: NZ$24M is Elementus's estimate as quoted by Wikipedia. Up to 900,000 users is an upper bound.

chip.name: BITFINEX
chip.takenLong: 119,756 BTC taken from users' segregated wallets (a Justice Department-based report gives 119,754)
chip.how: Coins left users' segregated wallets even though BitGo multi-signature security was in use.
chip.lesson: Multi-signature only helps if the whole signing setup is sound.
chip.outcome: In 2022 US authorities seized about 94,000 BTC (then $3.6B); two people later pleaded guilty to laundering.
chip.note: Wikipedia says 119,756 BTC; The Record says 119,754. How the signing was bypassed is not explained in either source, so the card does not say.

sources.title: The Record: DOJ seizes $3.6 billion from 2016 Bitfinex hack

block.name: COINCHECK
block.takenLong: About 523 million NEM sent out of one Coincheck NEM address
block.usdText: about $400 to $530 million at the time (58 billion yen)
block.how: About 523 million NEM tokens were sent out of one of the exchange's NEM addresses in a single night.
block.lesson: An exchange that can repay users from its own funds keeps its customers.
block.outcome: Coincheck repaid all 260,000 affected users in yen from its own funds, about 46.3 billion yen.
block.note: Wikipedia says "approximately 500 million NEM"; the AFP-based report quotes the exchange's 523 million. USD varies with the NEM price: $400M to $530M. Whether the coins sat in a hot wallet without multi-sig is widely reported but not stated in the fetched sources, so the card does not say.

sources.title: Security Affairs: Coincheck refunds customers (58 billion yen, 523 million NEM, 46.3 billion yen refund)

artifact.name: BYBIT
artifact.takenLong: About 400,000 ETH (Bybit's chief executive said 401,000) taken during a cold-to-warm wallet transfer
artifact.usdText: roughly $1.4 to $1.5 billion at the time
artifact.how: A wallet signing screen was manipulated, so approvers saw the right address while the code did something else.
artifact.lesson: Check what you are really signing, not just what the screen shows.
artifact.outcome: The FBI attributed it to North Korea-linked actors. It was the record until October 2026.
artifact.note: The FBI alert states only "approximately $1.5 billion". The 400,000 ETH figure comes from Wikipedia ("about 400,000 ETH") and Bybit's CEO (401,000 ETH). Bybit replacing the stolen funds is widely reported but is not in the fetched sources, so the card does not say it. "A third party's signing tool (Safe{Wallet}) was compromised" is Wikipedia's account, Bybit's own first report did not name it.

sources.title: FBI IC3 PSA I-022625: North Korea responsible for the Bybit theft
The Record: Hackers drained Bybit crypto exchange (21 Feb 2025)

bitcoin.name: BINANCE
bitcoin.takenLong: About $6.3 billion across ten blockchains, the largest crypto heist on record
bitcoin.usdText: about $6.3 billion as reported (other counts: $6.36B and $6.43B)
bitcoin.how: As reported: attackers drained hot wallets on ten chains in minutes; Binance first blamed a staff laptop.
bitcoin.lesson: Freeze fast, absorb the loss, and show proof of reserves.
bitcoin.outcome: About $3B in stablecoins was frozen; withdrawals reopened 1 Nov; Binance says users will not bear the loss.
bitcoin.note: Attribution to North Korea-linked actors is by the FBI and TRM Labs and is described in Wikipedia as alleged: keep "alleged". Still unfolding; the cause is not settled (laptop first; "other issues later found"; the EIP-7702 description is inconsistent). Frozen: ~$3B per Wikipedia (range $2.7 to $3B), Elliptic verified $2.85B frozen or seized per The Register. Replenished: 90% on 31 Oct (Wikipedia), ~95% by 2 Nov (The Register). Re-check at build time.

wild.name: COLD STORAGE
wild.place: Offline, out of reach of the internet
wild.takenLong: A sealed cold wallet: keys kept offline
wild.how: The defence: a cold wallet is kept offline, so its keys cannot be taken from a connected server.
wild.lesson: Keys that never touch the internet cannot be stolen over it.
wild.outcome: Why exchanges keep most customer coins offline and only a small float in hot wallets.
wild.note: Wikipedia: a cold wallet "remains offline and disconnected from the internet"; cold storage means "keeping the private keys out of reach of hackers". Bybit 2025 shows cold wallets can still be tricked at signing.

scatter.name: MT. GOX
scatter.takenLong: About 850,000 BTC (almost 750,000 customers' and about 100,000 its own), roughly 7% of all bitcoin then in existence; 200,000 were later found, leaving about 650,000
scatter.usdText: about 7% of all bitcoin then in existence
scatter.how: Cause still debated: withdrawals froze 7 February 2014; it filed for bankruptcy on 28 February.
scatter.lesson: Not your keys, not your coins.
scatter.outcome: Once handling over 70% of all bitcoin trades, it was bankrupt within weeks of halting withdrawals.
scatter.note: No USD figure for 2014 is stated in the fetched sources, so none is shown; the share of all bitcoin is used instead. The 2011 first breach: accounts worth more than $8.75M affected, price briefly fell to one cent on 19 June 2011.

vault.name: QUADRIGACX
vault.place: Vancouver-founded, run from Nova Scotia, Canada
vault.takenLong: About C$250 million owed to about 115,000 customers, missing or inaccessible (C$215.7M liabilities at the April 2019 bankruptcy filing)
vault.how: Not a hack: the founder died in December 2018, and its cold wallets had held nothing since April 2018.
vault.lesson: Ask for proof of reserves: empty vaults look full until someone checks.
vault.outcome: In June 2020 the Ontario Securities Commission concluded it was a fraud and a Ponzi scheme.
vault.note: Wikipedia: the five cold-wallet addresses examined by Ernst & Young had contained no cryptocurrency since April 2018; the OSC called it "an old-fashioned fraud wrapped in modern technology". The collapse became public in January 2019. Wikipedia does not call it a hack.

glossary.line: A wallet connected to the internet so an exchange can pay withdrawals fast. Convenient, and the usual target.
A wallet kept offline and disconnected from the internet, so its keys are out of reach of online attackers.
A wallet that needs a set number of independent keys to approve each transaction.
A public check that an exchange really holds the coins it owes customers. Binance said it would show its on 2 November 2026.
glossary.note: General definition written for this machine; no dedicated reference page was reachable. The 2 November 2026 statement is from the Binance 2026 article.

glossary.line: Naming who is behind a theft. An investigator's attribution, such as the FBI's to North Korea-linked actors, is shown as alleged unless a court has ruled. The museum names no attackers.

rules: Amounts are "at the time" and ranges are shown where sources disagree.
No individual hacker is named or shown; attribution is shown as alleged where sources say so.
